blocks.html:
This journey, like §12.6 and §13.3, introduces no new method. It carries one time-to-event question to a reported hazard ratio with the tools of §14.1–14.6, in the order a real survival analysis takes: describe follow-up, plot, test crudely, model, check assumptions, interpret and report.

Research question. Among households newly enrolled in a CBHI scheme, is receiving a community education intervention associated with the hazard of dropout, independent of household income and distance to the nearest facility?

Study design. A cohort of 300 newly enrolled CBHI households (data/cohort_dropout.csv), 153 of whom received the intervention, followed for up to 24 months. 120 dropped out; 18 moved away; 162 were still enrolled at 24 months. Total follow-up was 5,329.4 household-months, a crude dropout rate of 2.25 per 100 household-months.

Outcome. Time to dropout in months, with an event indicator (1 = dropped out, 0 = censored). Households that moved away or were still enrolled at 24 months are censored (recall §14.2). Treating moving away as censoring assumes a household that moved could still have dropped out afterwards; §14.8 checks what happens if it is instead a competing event.

Predictors/exposure. Intervention (1 = received, 0 = not) is the exposure. Income (Rs 1,000 per month; SD 4.42) and distance (km; SD 3.0) are covariates, chosen on substantive grounds as plausible confounders of both intervention uptake and dropout.

Why this method? A censored time-to-event outcome with several predictors. Ordinary regression cannot handle censoring (recall §14.1); the log-rank test cannot adjust for continuous covariates (recall §14.5). With 120 events and 3 predictors, there are 40 events per predictor, well above the convention of 10 (§14.6).

Crude analysis. The Kaplan–Meier curves (Figure 14.4a) separate early and stay apart: at 24 months, 0.66 of intervention households and 0.51 of the others were still enrolled. Neither curve reaches 0.5, so the median time to dropout is not reached in either group; retention at 24 months is the summary. The log-rank test gives χ² = 6.63, 1 df, p = 0.01 (§14.5). A Cox model with the intervention alone gives the crude HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.43–0.90).

Model specification. A Cox model with intervention, income and distance, all retained on substantive grounds rather than by automated selection.

Assumptions. Proportional hazards was checked two ways. The log(−log S) curves of the two groups run roughly parallel against log time (Figure 14.4b); the early steps are erratic because few events have occurred. The Schoenfeld residual test gives intervention p = 0.60 and global p = 0.35 (§14.6.2). Censoring is assumed non-informative: the 18 households that moved away are assumed no more or less likely to drop out than similar households that stayed.

Diagnostics. Dropping any one household changes the intervention HR only within 0.57 to 0.59 (dfbeta residuals: the change in a coefficient when that subject is removed). Income and distance are almost uncorrelated (r = 0.08), so collinearity is not a concern.

blocks.caption: Figure 14.4. CBHI cohort by intervention group. (a) Kaplan–Meier retention with censoring ticks; neither curve falls to 0.5, so both medians are not reached. (b) log(−log S(t)) against log(months): the roughly constant vertical gap supports proportional hazards.

library(survival)
co <- read.csv("data/cohort_dropout.csv")
crude <- coxph(Surv(time_months, dropout) ~ intervention, data = co)
fc <- coxph(Surv(time_months, dropout) ~ intervention + income_k +
              distance_km, data = co)
round(summary(crude)$conf.int, 2)
summary(fc)
             exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
intervention      0.62        1.6      0.43       0.9
...
  n= 300, number of events= 120 

                 coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)    
intervention -0.54161   0.58181  0.18773 -2.885  0.00391 ** 
income_k     -0.06224   0.93965  0.02177 -2.858  0.00426 ** 
distance_km   0.10793   1.11397  0.02749  3.927 8.61e-05 ***
...
             exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
intervention    0.5818     1.7188    0.4027    0.8406
income_k        0.9397     1.0642    0.9004    0.9806
distance_km     1.1140     0.8977    1.0555    1.1756
...
Likelihood ratio test= 26.45  on 3 df,   p=8e-06
Wald test            = 26.16  on 3 df,   p=9e-06
Score (logrank) test = 27  on 3 df,   p=6e-06

coef is the log-HR; exp(coef) is the HR; z = coef/SE (−0.5416/0.1877 = −2.885); the CI is exp(b ± 1.96 SE) = exp(−0.542 ± 0.368) = 0.40 to 0.84. exp(-coef) is the inverted HR, 1.72 (§14.6.1). The crude model’s score test equals the log-rank test (6.64 against 6.63, differing only in how tied times are handled).

Interpretation. Adjusting for income and distance, households that received the intervention had a 42% lower hazard of dropout at any point during follow-up than those that did not (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.40–0.84). This is a hazard: the instantaneous dropout rate among households still enrolled (recall §14.3), not the cumulative risk by 24 months. The HR moved from 0.62 (crude) to 0.58 (adjusted), a small shift. Each extra Rs 1,000 of monthly income went with a 6% lower hazard, and each extra km with an 11% higher hazard. Since PH was supported, one HR summarises the whole follow-up.

What the result does not mean. HR 0.58 is not “42% lower risk of dropping out by 24 months”. The cumulative dropout gap is a separate quantity: the crude risk ratio at 24 months is 0.69 (§14.6.1), because cumulative risk also depends on the baseline hazard, which this model leaves unspecified. Nor does this observational association show that the intervention causes lower dropout. Households that accepted it may differ in unmeasured ways (motivation, trust in the health system) that this analysis could not adjust for.

Reporting. “Of 300 households followed for up to 24 months, 120 dropped out; median time to dropout was not reached (58% still enrolled at 24 months). In a Cox proportional hazards model adjusting for household income and distance to the nearest facility, receipt of the community education intervention was associated with a lower hazard of CBHI dropout (crude HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.90; adjusted HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.40–0.84; p = 0.004). Proportional hazards was supported graphically and by Schoenfeld residuals (global p = 0.35). Given the observational design, a causal effect of the intervention cannot be established from this analysis alone.”

points.html: Report the crude comparison (Kaplan–Meier, log-rank, crude HR) and the adjusted HR. The first shows the unadjusted difference; the second shows what remains after adjustment.
State the median, or say it is not reached and give S(t) at fixed times.
Check PH before leading with a single HR.
Keep “hazard” and “risk” apart throughout, and state the causal caveat in the same paragraph as the main result.
